text:
As the Denver Broncos ramp up the intensity of training camp over the past two days, we've seen two key players limp off the field with injuries.

On Tuesday — Day 4 of Broncos camp — Pro Bowl outside linebacker Nik Bonitto exited practice early, limping off the field surrounding by trainers. He was carrying his own weight, with a limp, and there was no cart needed.

The injury came during a 9-on-7 drill in the Broncos' second padded practice of training camp, per 9NEWS' Mike Klis. Afterward, the very first question head coach Sean Payton got was about the Bonitto injury.

"He'll be fine," Payton said of Bonitto. "No updates."

Payton is always tight-lipped about injuries, and unless it's something serious, don't expect him to elaborate further. Go ahead and exhale now because Payton said Bonitto is going to be okay.

The injury could cause the fifth-year pro to miss some camp practices. The Broncos would be remiss to rush him back on the field, considering how Bonitto is their franchise edge rusher.

A Gradual Ramp-Up to Training Camp

Before Bonitto's injury, Broncos starting center Luke Wattenberg exited Monday's padded practice in pain and did not return. Likewise, Payton said at the podium that Wattenberg "will be fine," and the fifth-year center was out there for Tuesday's practice, though he wasn't in pads.

The Broncos' gradual approach to this training camp, as we're learning, was wise. Instead of hitting the grass hard last week as soon as the veterans reported, the Broncos held two "acclimation" practice days. Friday was the first official day of training camp, and with each practice, the team has increased the intensity and duration of the sessions.

After four straight practices, counting the two "acclimation" days, the Broncos rested on Sunday. Monday was the first padded practice; Tuesday was the second, and it went a little bit longer.

Tuesday's padded practice was also more intense. Tempers flew as the camp emotions begin to boild to the surface as the intensity rises.

"Second day in pads," Payton said afterward on Wednesday. "A little bit longer practice. We had some competitive periods at the end."

It was certainly competitive, as illustrated by the scuffle that broke out between tight end Evan Engram and nickel cornerback Ja'Quan McMillian. Day 4? Sounds about right for the first squabble among teammates.

Bonitto's Outlook

Bonitto, 26, is coming off his second consecutive Pro Bowl season, posting a career-high 14 sacks in 2025. Right before the regular season started, the Broncos extended him, signing him to a four-year, $106 million deal that keeps him under contract through the 2029 season.

Bonitto could be poised to take another big step forward in 2026, as some national outlets have tapped him as a Defensive Player of the Year candidate and a potential sack champion. His goals are to simply improve "all facets" of his game in Year 5.

"All facets," Bonitto told the team website in July. "I still have a lot of room to grow in my game — in the run and in the pass. Just keep trying to fine-tune these things, keep looking at other guys around the league that are doing it at a high level and seeing how I can put it into my game to continue to be the best player I know I can be."

In order for Bonitto to have a shot at those achievements, he'll need to be healthy.

Last year, Bonitto produced at a high level, despite playing the entire season with a wrist injury. He underwent minor surgery this offseason to repair the wrist.

Bonitto is a warrior, no doubt, and a big contributor to the Broncos' massive turnaround over the past two years.

Hopefully, Bonitto will be back on the field this week some time. Best not to rush it, though.

title: The cascading effect of Coby Bryant's injury leaves Bears more problems to solve
description:
He had what Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen decided they needed most — speed.
And his addition made the Bears more comfortable drafting a first-round safety, Dillon Thieneman, to pair with him.
The cascading effect of the injury gives the Bears a problem to solve.
He’s entering his second season as the Bears’ defensive coordinator and has still never held a single training-camp practice with his starting defensive backs healthy.
Allen said the Bears won’t “put any higher expectations” on the first-round pick with Bryant gone.
text:
In an austere offseason, Coby Bryant was the splurge.

The Bears bet big on him, letting All-Pro safety Kevin Byard and four-year starter Jaquan Brisker leave this offseason, and giving him a three-year, $40 million deal.

The safety had been where the Bears want to go — the Super Bowl. He had what Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen decided they needed most — speed. And his addition made the Bears more comfortable drafting a first-round safety, Dillon Thieneman, to pair with him.

It took less than an hour on the first day of padded practice Monday for all that to crumble. Bryant hyperextended his left knee, -suffering a bone bruise and a small break that will keep him out eight to 10 weeks.

The cascading effect of the injury gives the Bears a problem to solve. Or, rather, many problems.

It will take creativity from Allen and -flexibility from the players.

“I mean, that’s all of our jobs,” Allen said Tuesday. “That’s the coaches’ job, that’s the players’ job. You know nothing ever goes exactly how you planned, right? You have to be able to adjust.”

Life after Bryant will be nothing new for Allen. He’s entering his second season as the Bears’ defensive coordinator and has still never held a single training-camp practice with his starting defensive backs healthy. Cornerback Jaylon Johnson hurt his groin training in the weeks before camp began last year. Nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon, who was out most of last season, began this year’s training camp on the Physically unable-to-perform list with a calf injury.

Then there’s Thieneman, the rookie whose transition to the NFL was supposed to be eased by the very presence of Bryant. Allen said the Bears won’t “put any higher expectations” on the first-round pick with Bryant gone. His absence, though, risks stunting Thieneman’s growth. That’s the most alarming possibility among the many consequences of Bryant’s injury.

“We’ve got Dillon that’s going to have big big shoes to fill,” linebacker Devin Bush said. “Him being a rookie, he’s got to come up to speed.”

Bryant’s injury is a Gordon problem, too. Bears coaches have been annoyed for months by Gordon’s slow recovery. When he wasn’t healthy enough to start camp, the Bears were forced to play safety Cam Lewis, whom they signed away from the Bills in March, at slot cornerback. Lewis played 145 of his 373 defensive snaps in the slot last year — and the rest at safety. His versatility was his greatest strength. Now Lewis will be penciled into a starting safety position opposite Thieneman.

That could change, if safety Elijah Hicks returns after starting training camp on the PUP list with shin pain. General manager Ryan Poles expected a quick recovery for Hicks, who started seven games in 2024 when Brisker was concussed. The Bears added depth Tuesday by signing safety Marlen Sewell, who won a brief look from the Chiefs coming out of their tryout camp. For now, at least, the Bears are unlikely to try to trade for help at the position.

With Lewis at safety, veteran Jaylon Jones, the team’s third-string slot cornerback, played with the starters during Tuesday’s practice. Special-teams ace Josh Blackwell can play in the slot, too, but the Bears coaching staff rarely used him last year when injuries ravaged his position. He played just three defensive snaps. Fourth-round pick Malik Muhammad is learning how to play the nickel position but has a long way to go.

Playing the slot is different than being outside. To react quickly, you need to know where to keep your eyes. That takes practice.

“If you put your eyes in the right spot,” -Allen said, “you have a chance to be right.”

And many more chances to be wrong.

Staff report

FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — Former Salisbury High and Georgia Bulldog star Jalon Walker may have torn an ACL near the end of the Atlanta Falcons’ practice on Tuesday.

Walker will have an MRI on Wednesday.

He sustained the injury during an 11-on-11, two-minute drill period. He went to the ground in the backfield and remained there while teammates surrounded him on their knees. After evaluation from the Falcons’ training staff, Walker was carted off the field and the team called off the rest of practice.

If Walker did indeed tear a ligament in his knee, he will almost certainly miss the entire 2026 season.

The edge rusher was the 15th pick in the 2025 NFL draft and had a strong rookie season for the Falcons.

Walker appeared in 15 games as a rookie and started nine. He accumulated four sacks in four games from Weeks 9-12. At season’s end, the Georgia product had logged 36 tackles, 5.5 sacks, nine QB hits and two forced fumbles.
